title: Venezuela Releases Political Prisoners as Calls for Elections Grow
summary:
Venezuelan authorities released a number of political prisoners early Saturday morning, according to the human rights group Foro Penal. The releases came days after Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, met U.S. President Donald Trump at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday. Trump captured former President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year.

Among those freed was Wilder Vasquez, who was sentenced to five years in 2018 over claims he was plotting to kill Maduro. Foro Penal also confirmed the release of Miguel Castillo Cedeño, who it says was arbitrarily detained since June 2019, and Frank Cabañas, who rights groups say had been held for nine years after being linked to the death of a police officer. Gonzalo Himiob, vice-president of Foro Penal, said "a significant number" of political prisoners had been released from several detention centers.

Rodríguez's administration had already released hundreds of prisoners as part of a reconciliation effort following Maduro's seizure. But the releases slowed to a trickle in April after she said the scheme was "coming to an end," drawing criticism from opposition and rights groups. Foro Penal said the program stopped with less than half of the nation's political prisoners released.

Venezuela's government has not commented on the latest releases or said whether they resulted from Rodríguez's conversation with Trump. It continues to deny that dissidents are jailed and has cast the releases as a gesture of goodwill. Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, a close ally of Maduro, called the meeting with Trump "a great triumph of the diplomacy of peace." But opposition voices criticized the meeting, seeing it as ignoring their calls — which the U.S. has previously endorsed — for swift elections. Rodríguez has tried to present her interim government as more open to political dissent while building favor with the United States.
why_it_matters: Decisions in Caracas about who stays in prison and whether elections happen shape the daily freedoms of millions of people, and this case tests whether international pressure — like the meeting Rodríguez used — can actually change an authoritarian government's behavior.

background_read: Venezuela is a country on the northern coast of South America, and Nicolás Maduro (its president from 2013 until he was removed this year) led a government that critics call authoritarian; the United States has long pressured him with sanctions and criminal charges.

Delcy Rodríguez (who became Venezuela's interim president after Maduro's removal) served for years as his vice president, and Diosdado Cabello (the interior minister and a longtime ally of Maduro) still helps run the government.

Foro Penal (a Venezuelan human rights group) is one of the few organizations that keeps a public count of political prisoners, because the government itself denies that anyone is jailed for political reasons.

Many countries, including the United States, argue that Venezuela's 2024 presidential election was not fair — a dispute that sits in the background of these releases and the renewed calls for fresh elections.

perspectives.description: The releases are presented as a gesture of goodwill and as proof that talking directly to Washington pays off. Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello even calls the Trump meeting 'a great triumph of the diplomacy of peace,' letting the interim government claim credit at home and abroad.

Foro Penal says the program stopped with less than half of Venezuela's political prisoners freed, and the government still denies that dissidents are jailed at all. Critics argue the releases are a public-relations move that ignores their central demand: swift, free elections.

Governments under international pressure often release a limited number of prisoners when they want sanctions eased or legitimacy restored. Partial releases let them look reforming while keeping pressure on the opponents who remain locked up.

The real test is whether releases continue and whether Rodríguez moves toward the elections the U.S. has endorsed. If the prisoner count stops falling, outside pressure — and possibly new sanctions — is likely to return.
